$description: Tier 2 — semantic/alias tokens. The PUBLIC contract apps consume.

primary.$description: Button/CTA fill. MUST stay dark enough to carry white label text at AA in EVERY theme — that is why the dark theme sits on 500 and not on a lighter step, and why hover goes DARKER (600) rather than lighter. Text links use color.action.link instead, which is free to lighten on dark surfaces. Enforced by test/mode-contrast.test.mjs; the dark theme shipped white-on-#2d84e8 at 3.77:1 until 2026-08.

primaryScale.$description: Full mode-aware primary ramp (50–900). Consume via --sa-color-primaryScale-50…950. Each step follows the active brand.

secondaryScale.$description: Full mode-aware SECONDARY ramp (50–900) = Figma Secondary/*. BRAND-INVARIANT since 2026-08-11 — India Saffron in both brands. Consume via --sa-color-secondaryScale-*.

accentScale.$description: ACCENT brand scale — India Green #046A38 from the SAMAVESH logo. Brand-INVARIANT (blue and navy resolve to identical values), and deliberately the same green as color.successScale: two greens nine degrees apart is a defect whichever token owns them.

neutralScale.$description: Full mode-aware NEUTRAL ramp (0–1000) = Figma Palette/color/neutralScale/*. Hue-locked to the brand's own primary. Consume via --sa-color-neutralScale-*. Renumbered 2026-08-11 to match UX4G: pure white at 0, pure black at 1000, near-black at 950. There is no 1100 — the old top step was retired by that renumbering.

successScale.$description: Full SUCCESS ramp (50–900) = Figma Success/*. Mode-invariant (identical in Blue-Light and Blue-Dark). Consume via --sa-success-50…900.

dangerScale.$description: Full DANGER ramp (50–900) = Figma Danger/*. Mode-invariant. Consume via --sa-danger-50…900.

warningScale.$description: Full WARNING ramp (50–900) = Figma Warning/*. Mode-invariant. Consume via --sa-warning-50…900.

infoScale.$description: Full INFO ramp (50–900) = Figma Info/*. Mode-invariant. Consume via --sa-info-50…900.

transparent.$description: Alpha overlay tiers (8/16/24/32/40/48%), plus a 0 tier where a fade needs its far end (secondary, for the rail's identity wash, 2026-09-06). A 0 tier is added per family WITH its consumer — check:token-consumers refuses a token nothing binds. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs. Each tier is a colour REFERENCE plus an alpha/N REFERENCE — never an rgba() literal, because 48 literals is exactly the shape of thing that silently keeps a retired colour alive, and because a literal cannot follow a brand. In CSS a tier resolves as color-mix(in srgb, var(base) calc(var(--sa-alpha-N) * 100%), transparent); in Figma it is an alias to the base variable with its opacity bound to alpha/N. Consume via --sa-color-transparent-<family>-<step>.

0.$description: The far end of a fade: secondary at 0%. A gradient that dissolves into nothing needs a bound stop of the SAME hue at zero alpha — in Figma a bound gradient stop takes its variable's alpha, so `transparent` has to be a variable too. Never used as a fill on its own.

disabled.$description: Disabled label ink. OPAQUE, and one rung darker than the 48% wash it replaced: rgba(30,33,36,.48) composited to #939496, which measured 1.83:1 on bg/neutral/disabled — a disabled button whose label could not be read at all. neutralScale/400 is 3.06:1 on white and 2.68:1 on the disabled fill: legible, and still unmistakably inactive. WCAG exempts disabled controls (1.4.3), so this is a floor the estate sets for itself, not a conformance claim. Follows the brand's neutral hue, and DBIM's pure greys under a dbim-* mode, by reference.

a11y.$description: Accessibility-widget self-contained palettes (its own HC + dark toggles).

color.$description: Tier 2 colour, two generations side by side: the canonical grammar namespace (bg/*, text/*, border/*, icon/*, on/*, layer/*) is authored in system.generated.json from the ramps; this group holds the brand-varying scales (primaryScale…infoScale — Tier 1 in disguise, never bound in app code), the alias-plus-alpha transparent tiers (color/transparent/<family>/<alpha>), the action/status/brand/text legacy roles the --ds-* era named, and the a11y staging values. New work binds the grammar namespace; the legacy roles are kept for the components that still read them and are listed for sunset in the colour audit.

density.$description: Density token set: control height per density mode.

font.$description: Tier-2 font roles. Apps must reach for these, never for the Tier-1 --sa-ref-font-family-* primitives: a component bound to a primitive cannot be re-fonted by a brand pack. Added when the tier lint caught the design-system typography page referencing the Devanagari primitive directly.

devanagari.$description: Devanagari/Hindi text. Pair with lang=hi on the element. Never italic — the script has no italic tradition and slanting degrades legibility.

latin.$description: The estate default for Latin text. Tier-2 alias so a brand pack can re-font without touching components.

display.$description: The optical Display cut, for the 40-80px Display ramp. In Figma this is a STYLE of Noto Sans (Display Medium), not a separate family.

mono.$description: Tabular and code contexts. A system stack, deliberately not a webfont.

weight.$description: Tier-2 font weights. They were Tier-1 `ref/font/weight/*` until 2026-08-26, and that was the whole reason 24 of the library's text styles bound a reference token: a text style has to name a cut, and no Tier-2 cut existed to name. They are a ROLE, not a raw step — a brand pack that ships a heavier body face changes them here, and every style follows. Figma has no numeric weight, so the build projects each one to the STYLE NAME its family is addressed by (see FIGMA_FONT_STYLES).

light.$description: 300 — the ICON cut, and the only place the estate uses it. Every Figma `Icon/*` text style is Material Symbols Rounded / Light and `<Icon>` defaults to 300, so this is the one token both read. NOT for prose: 300 on Noto Sans at body sizes thins the stroke below what the ramp is drawn for.

regular.$description: Body copy and anything that is read rather than scanned.

medium.$description: Titles and labels — the weight that separates a heading from its paragraph without shouting.

semibold.$description: Headlines, and the emphasised cut of body copy.

bold.$description: Reserved. The estate's headings stop at semibold; bold is for the rare in-line emphasis a heading cannot carry.

displayMedium.$description: The Display cut at Medium — 500 on `Noto Sans Display` for the 40-80px ramp. It is a SEPARATE token from `medium` because Figma does not model the Display cut as a family: it is the STYLE string "Display Medium" of Noto Sans, which is why the build special-cases this one name instead of projecting 500 to "Medium". In CSS the same pairing is `font/display` plus this weight.

icon.$description: Material Symbols Rounded — the face every icon glyph renders in. Bind this from `.material-symbols-rounded`, never the Tier-1 primitive. The `@font-face` rule in icons.css still names the family literally because a font-face descriptor cannot take a custom property; that literal is the font LOADER, this token is what everything else reads.

brand.$description: MARK COLOURS — the fixed palette of a logo, not a role in the interface. They are Tier 2 and they alias NOTHING, which is the one place in this file where a literal is the correct answer: a mark does not re-colour when the brand pack changes, because the mark IS the brand. That is also why they belong in the mode-less Static collection rather than in Color — a value that must never move should not sit in a collection whose whole purpose is moving. Authored here on 2026-08-26; the library had carried them as hand-made `ref/brand/*` variables since before the pipeline, with a codeSyntax pointing at `--sa-ref-brand-samavesh-*` names that had never existed in any stylesheet. USE THEM ONLY inside the mark they belong to. The SAMAVESH ink is #1F2428 and the estate's text ink is #1E2124 — two colours that look identical in review and are not the same, which is exactly why the mark needs its own token rather than borrowing `text/neutral/base`.

ink.$description: The wordmark's own ink. NOT `text/neutral/base` (#1E2124) — close enough to pass a glance, far enough to be a defect.

purple.$description: DigiLocker's own purple, for the DigiLocker lockup only. A partner's colour is theirs, so it is a constant here and never a role.

devanagari.$description: Body-1's Devanagari line height, for a Hindi block that has no role of its own. Every role carries its own type/<role>/lhDevanagari — the Latin leading plus a fifth of the size, on the 4px grid — and a Hindi block bound to a role takes THAT, at the same size as its Latin sibling. Until 2026-09-04 this was a unitless 1.7 applied to every Hindi block: it undid the scale (a 40px headline at 68px leading) and Figma read it as 1.7px.

leading.$description: Line-height rules that are not a role — today only the Devanagari leading, derived per role by the build.

hover.$description: The neutral hover wash — a row, a menu item, a plain icon button responding to the pointer. Same rung as bg/neutral/subtler by design: hover on a neutral surface is one step of tint, not a new colour. Bind this, not subtler, so a hover can be retuned without moving every quiet surface.

active.$description: The neutral pressed wash — one step past hover, held while the pointer is down or the row is being acted on. Pairs with bg/neutral/hover the way overlay/brand/active pairs with overlay/brand/hover.

selected.$description: The selected row, item or navigation entry — the brand's lightest tint, so selection reads as ‘chosen’ rather than ‘hovered’ even on a neutral list. The sidebar's current page and a data table's chosen row bind it. Selected is a STATE the reader set; hover is one the pointer set.

readonly.$description: A read-only field's ground: quieter than an editable field, and NOT the disabled fill — the value is the point and stays readable and selectable. forms.css binds it on [readonly] inputs.

loading.$description: The resting fill of a loading skeleton, under the shimmer — a surface in its LOADING state. Its own role so a skeleton can be retuned without touching the surfaces it stands in for; motion/loading/pulse carries the shimmer's timing.

bg.$description: Background fills by family and prominence. base is the page; subtler/subtle are tints; bold/bolder/boldest are solid fills that carry the on/* ink.

default.$description: Text-link colour. Decoupled from action.primary so it can be lighter on dark surfaces (≥4.5:1 as text) without weakening white-on-primary button contrast. BLUE IS RAMP 600, NOT 500, and the reason is the ground it actually sits on: 500 (#0373df) measures 4.64:1 on white but 4.07:1 on bg/surface/muted, which is the class the estate's own <body> carries — so the link failed 1.4.3 on most pages while passing every check. 600 (#005eb9) is 6.36:1 and 5.57:1. It passed because the contrast contract judges text against bg/neutral/base, i.e. white; that surface assumption is recorded as an open item rather than widened here, since widening it re-judges every text token at once. Navy holds ramp 500 through its own colorModes override and already clears 4.5:1 on that ground. dbim has no such override, so it follows the base step and moved to 600 with it across all six of its hues — which only darkens those links, never lightens them.

text.$description: Text inks by family and prominence. base is body copy; subtle is captions; subtler is non-essential; bolder/boldest are headings that must hit AA/AAA.

default.$description: Form control border, resting. Rung 500 since 2026-09-04: rung 400 (#8e949c) was 3.06:1 on white — a hairline pass of 1.4.11 — and 2.68:1 on bg/neutral/subtler, the ground most forms actually sit on, which is a FAIL. 500 measures 4.65:1 on white and 4.07:1 on the muted ground. Hover steps to 600.

Border/rule ink on a dark or brand surface — the inverse of border/neutral/base. Nested as inverse/default rather than a bare `inverse` leaf because it has a `subtle` sibling, which is the same shape border/neutral/bolder already uses (bolder/default, bolder/hover). Aliases `color/neutralScale/0`, as `subtle` does, so the pair moves together if the neutral ramp's white is ever retuned.

subtle.$description: The quieter inverse rule — white (neutralScale/0) at alpha/40, authored as a reference plus an opacity reference since 2026-09-04 rather than a pre-composited rgba(). Used by Divider Tone=Inverse subtle and the AccessibilityBar's separators. The Figma variable was `border/neutral/inverse-subtle` until 2026-08-18 — a hyphen inside a segment, which grammar RULE 1 forbids; renamed IN PLACE so bindings followed.

inverse.$description: Borders drawn on an inverse (dark) surface — the footer, a tooltip, a bold status band.

selected.$description: The edge of a selected control — a checked selection card, a chosen chip, a current tab's rail. Brand 500, the same rung as focus/ring, so ‘selected’ and ‘focused’ share a colour and differ by geometry (a ring stands off the control; this edge is the control's own).

border.$description: Edge colours by family and prominence, plus the resting/hover control border.

ring.$description: The keyboard focus ring. SOLID since 2026-09-04: it was rgba(3,115,223,.48), which flattens on white to #86bcf0 — 2.01:1 against the 3:1 that WCAG 2.2 1.4.11 asks of a focus indicator — and 53 outline rules across chips, search, controls and the auth stack still read it after forms.css alone was corrected on 2026-09-03. It now aliases the brand key colour, which is 4.64:1 on white and 4.07:1 on the muted page in Blue, and follows Navy and the DBIM modes through the alias. Paint it as `outline: var(--sa-focus-width) solid var(--sa-focus-ring)` with `outline-offset: var(--sa-focus-offset)`, never as a box-shadow — a shadow is not painted in Windows High Contrast Mode.

width.$description: The ring's thickness — `border/width/md` (2px). WCAG 2.4.13 asks for a 2px perimeter at minimum; this is that minimum, not a decoration.

offset.$description: The gap between the control's edge and the ring — `space/2`, so the ring never covers the control's own border and the two stay distinguishable.

focus.$description: The keyboard focus ring — colour, width and offset. WCAG 2.4.7's one non-optional affordance; a group, not a state, because it has three properties and one job.

ringInner.$description: The inner ring of a two-tone focus indicator — white, laid between the control and focus/ring so the ring stays visible on a brand or dark surface where blue-on-blue would vanish (WCAG 2.4.13 asks for 3:1 against adjacent colours). In CSS: box-shadow 0 0 0 focus/offset focus/ringInner, then the outline; in Figma the focus/ring effect style binds its inner spread to it.

boldest.$description: The scrim behind a modal — the brand's neutral 800 at alpha/48, as a REFERENCE plus an OPACITY reference. Until 2026-09-04 this was an rgba() literal with six hand-authored DBIM copies, because a literal in the single-mode Color collection is frozen at whatever brand was current when it was typed — and Navy once inherited the Blue neutral (#1E2124 for #1E2024) without anyone seeing it. Figma can now alias a colour and keep a separate opacity, so the copies are gone: the scrim follows neutralScale/800 through Blue, Navy and every DBIM mode by construction.

hover.$description: State layer for hover on a NEUTRAL surface — ink at 4%, laid over whatever the surface is. Material 3's hover layer; the brand counterpart is overlay/brand/hover. Use where a surface must keep its own colour under the interaction (an image tile, a coloured card) and bg/neutral/hover would replace it.

active.$description: State layer for pressed on a neutral surface — ink at 8%. One step past hover, like every pressed state in the system.

focus.$description: State layer for a focused surface that has no ring of its own — a focused list row, a focused card — ink at 16%. The ring (focus/ring) remains the primary focus indicator; this is the tint beneath it, never a replacement.

drag.$description: State layer for a surface being dragged — ink at 8%, with elevation/raised. A dragged row is lifted and tinted so it reads as detached from the list beneath it.

brand.$description: Translucent white washes for interactive states on a BRAND-coloured surface, where a solid hover fill would fight the brand. The family slot names the SURFACE, not the wash — the same reading as `on/bg/brand/*`, which is ink for a brand background rather than brand-coloured ink. Authored in Figma first as `overlay/on-brand/*`, a name the grammar rejects (a hyphen inside a path segment), which is exactly why it could never be generated and its codeSyntax named a CSS variable that did not exist.

hover.$description: Hover wash on a brand-coloured surface. 8%, matching the published Figma variable and the AccessibilityBar's States documentation. This family was authored here at 12% from a base that predated 33cbb4f, which had already corrected the component from 12% to 8%; reconciled to 8% on 2026-08-19.

active.$description: Pressed/selected wash on a brand-coloured surface. Named `active`, not `pressed` — `active` is the state word the whole system uses (cmp/action/*/active/bg), and the grammar has no `pressed`.

overlay.$description: Scrims and washes: the modal scrim (neutral/boldest) and the hover/active washes on brand-coloured surfaces. Each is a colour reference plus an alpha reference.

inline.$description: Horizontal gap between items on one line. VALUE-NAMED: `inline/16` is 16px, and 16px in every other family too. Every family carries the same ladder so no measurement is unexpressible — the old scale could not state a 20px gap or a 40px padding at all, and work reached past the layer to a hidden ref/space/* primitive instead.

stack.$description: Vertical gap between stacked items, and vertical rhythm inside a block. VALUE-NAMED: `stack/16` is 16px, and 16px in every other family too. Every family carries the same ladder so no measurement is unexpressible — the old scale could not state a 20px gap or a 40px padding at all, and work reached past the layer to a hidden ref/space/* primitive instead.

padding.$description: Inset between a container's edge and its content. VALUE-NAMED: `padding/16` is 16px, and 16px in every other family too. Every family carries the same ladder so no measurement is unexpressible — the old scale could not state a 20px gap or a 40px padding at all, and work reached past the layer to a hidden ref/space/* primitive instead.

section.$description: Vertical rhythm between page-level sections. VALUE-NAMED: `section/16` is 16px, and 16px in every other family too. Every family carries the same ladder so no measurement is unexpressible — the old scale could not state a 20px gap or a 40px padding at all, and work reached past the layer to a hidden ref/space/* primitive instead.

chart.$description:
Data-visualisation roles, and the one place in this system where a literal is sometimes the RIGHT answer — so each group states which it is and why, because the difference is not guessable from the values.

REFERENCES the system ramps: div/* (signed data) and trend/* (KPI direction). Both encode MEANING the rest of the UI already has a colour for — negative is what error means — so they follow it, and follow it into a DBIM conformance mode too.

LITERAL on purpose: cat/* (twelve categorical series) and seq/* (single-hue sequential ramp). Both are tuned as a SET for a job the UI ramps are not tuned for — mutual distinguishability and even perceptual steps respectively — and a reference would let one member drift out of that tuning on a brand swap. Their own descriptions carry the argument in full.

grid/axis/tooltip/region are structural. Theme-aware dark/hc overrides are retained on these tokens but NOT currently emitted: the appearance axis was retired on 2026-08-10 and the UX4G accessibility widget owns dark and high contrast (see build/formats/legacy-ds-css.mjs).

cat.$description:
Twelve categorical series. DELIBERATELY LITERAL, and deliberately NOT tracking the brand ramps — do not "fix" these into references. A categorical palette has one job: colours a reader can tell apart AT ONCE, which is a property of the SET, chosen and checked together. A reference would let one member move on its own: point cat/1 at primaryScale and a Blue-to-Navy brand swap slides it toward another blue, and two series in one chart become one. The set is fixed so that cannot happen.

RE-CUT 2026-09-04 by simulated annealing over all twelve slots at once, against six constraints held simultaneously: every slot OKLCH chroma >= 0.10 (four of the previous twelve sat at 0.08-0.09 and read as grey); every slot >= 3:1 on both the white card and the muted page; every slot at least dE 8 from each of the four status inks (the previous brown cat/2 sat dE 4 from the warning ink and the crimson cat/4 dE 7 from the error ink — a series that IS a status colour to the eye); adjacent slots >= dE 15 in ordinary vision (the previous 8 and 9 were 12.6); every pair among 1-9 at least dE 12.2 apart in ordinary vision (was 11.7); and, the ratchet, every pair among 1-9 >= dE 8 under protanopia, deuteranopia AND tritanopia (Machado 2009), now 8.22 against 8.04 before.

WHAT NINE COLOUR-BLIND-SAFE SLOTS COST, MEASURED. A dichromat keeps one chromatic axis plus lightness, so nine mutually distinct colours need lightness coding, and the search proves it: inside the OKLCH lightness band 43-77 that data-visualisation practice recommends, no nine-slot set reaches dE 8 on every pair (best found 7.5). Two slots therefore sit at L* 42.2-42.3, one point below the band, where four did before. Slots 1-6 are additionally kept >= 25 degrees apart in hue so the six a chart most often uses are six hues, not three at two lightnesses. A chart with more than six series should be small multiples or fold its tail into "Other" regardless.

SLOTS 1-9 ARE GUARANTEED mutually distinguishable including through every dichromacy; SLOTS 10-12 ARE EXTENSION COLOURS, distinct in full colour only. tools/chart-slot-order/check.mjs fails the build on a consumer reaching past 9. A series may share a hue family with a status colour (cat/2 is a red, cat/4 a green) — the dataviz reference palette does the same — because a status colour never carries meaning alone: it ships with its icon and its word, and a series never wears a status token. cat/1 is gov-blue #0373DF, the brand anchor, and is the one member that did not move. If this palette is ever re-cut, re-cut all twelve together and re-measure every property above — packages/tokens/test/chart-palette.test.mjs holds the numbers as ratchets.

seq.$description:
Single-hue sequential ramp for choropleths and heatmaps. DELIBERATELY LITERAL — do not point it at primaryScale, even though seq/500 is gov-blue exactly. The two ramps are tuned for different jobs and cannot share a ladder: primaryScale places its rungs by CONTRAST, so a named rung clears a WCAG threshold against its ink, while a sequential data ramp needs even PERCEPTUAL steps so equal differences in the data read as equal differences on the map. Rungs chosen for contrast produce a choropleth with a visible band where two adjacent buckets look identical and another where they jump. Ten steps here against primaryScale's eleven is the same story from the other end.

RE-SPACED 2026-09-04: the ladder was 6.9 / 9.4 / 9.7 / 8.3 / 5.0 / 7.3 / 7.5 / 7.9 / 7.8 L* per step — the 400->500 step was half its neighbours because 500 is pinned to gov-blue and the rest had been placed by eye — so two adjacent classes on a choropleth were closer than any other two. Steps are now 7.6-7.8 L* apart from 95.7 to 25.9, 500 still exactly #0373DF, chroma following the same arc the brand ramps use. A class scale should start at 100, not 50: 50 measures 1.01:1 against the muted page and exists as the lightest tint for a heatmap on a white card.

div.$description: Diverging scale for SIGNED data — negative through neutral to positive. The NEGATIVE wing references the danger ramp, for the reason chart/trend/* always has: "negative" here means exactly what "error" means everywhere else. The POSITIVE wing is the sequential BLUE since 2026-09-04, not the success green. Measured under deuteranopia — the most common colour-vision deficiency, about one man in twelve — the red and green wings were one colour: dE 4.1 at the strong ends, 7.9 at the mid steps, 1.7 at the soft steps, so a diverging map showed no direction at all to those readers. Red against blue measures dE 17.9 / 26.9 / 9.3 at the same three steps (the soft ends are meant to sit close to the neutral midpoint), which is why every published diverging scheme (ColorBrewer RdBu, the ONS and Census maps) is red-blue or purple-green rather than red-green. Blue also makes the diverging scale the sequential scale with a red wing added, so magnitude and sign read from one vocabulary. Rungs are chosen for LIGHTNESS SYMMETRY, measured: neg L* 64.4 / pos 64.3, negStrong 34.5 / posStrong 33.6, negSoft 86.6 / posSoft 87.9. The wing is brand-invariant because chart/seq is literal. div/mid follows the neutral ramp; see the note on chart neutrals elsewhere in this group.

trend.$description: 2026-09-04: up and down are rung 600, the same rung the status text and icons read, so an arrow in a metric-card pill and the success ink beside it are one colour. Under deuteranopia the pair measures dE 5.7 (it was 6.4 at rung 500): red against green is a property of the deficiency, not of any palette, and the direction is carried by the arrow and the sign, never by the colour alone.

grid.$description: Chart gridlines — neutral 100, quiet enough to sit beneath the data without competing with it.

axis.$description: Axis lines and tick labels — neutral 500, readable against white and distinct from the gridlines.

tooltipBg.$description: The tooltip surface — neutral 800, the inverse surface so a tooltip reads as a layer above the chart.

tooltipInk.$description: Tooltip text and values — white on `chart/tooltipBg`.

regionEmpty.$description: A map region with no reading — neutral 100, deliberately outside the sequential ramp so ‘no data’ can never be mistaken for a low value.

regionStroke.$description: Region boundaries on a choropleth — white, so two adjacent shaded regions separate.

code.$description:
Code and terminal specimens — the chrome a documentation page needs in order to SHOW code, which until now every docs page hand-rolled. The same six hexes were copied into two pages independently, which is exactly the drift the design system exists to stop.

LITERAL on purpose, like chart/cat/* and chart/seq/*: this palette is tuned as a SET against its own background for token-level legibility, not against the page. Referencing the UI ramps would let one member drift out of that tuning on a brand swap and quietly wreck the contrast the set was built for.

DELIBERATELY DARK IN EVERY THEME. A terminal specimen that flips to a light surface stops reading as a terminal, so there are no colorModes or themes overrides here — the block looks the same under blue, navy, dbim, light and dark. It is chrome around a specimen, not a UI surface.

Every foreground role clears WCAG AA against code/bg, measured: text 12.95:1, string 11.37:1, builtin 9.58:1, keyword 6.04:1, comment 5.09:1. Comment is the floor and has the least headroom — if it is ever lightened, re-measure.

bg.$description: The block surface. Dark in every theme, on purpose.

text.$description: Default code foreground — plain identifiers, punctuation, shell output. 12.95:1.

comment.$description: Comments and shell prompt annotations (the # lines). 5.09:1 — the lowest-contrast role in the set, and still AA.

keyword.$description: Language keywords — import, from, const, export. 6.04:1.

builtin.$description: The executable or callee in a command — npm, node, git. 9.58:1.

shell.$description: The terminal WINDOW around the code body — deliberately a step darker than code/bg so the titlebar reads as chrome and the code reads as content. The two were #12141c and #1e2130 chosen independently in two files; this pair makes that relationship intentional.

border.$description: Hairline around the terminal window and under its titlebar. Alpha-on-dark rather than a solid, so it holds up if the shell colour is ever retuned.

chrome.$description: The titlebar strip fill — barely-there lift off code/shell.

chromeText.$description: Titlebar label and the resting state of the copy button. White at alpha/48 — 4.97:1 on code/shell, AA for the UI text it carries (was 45%, 4.52:1, before the scale was rationalised on 2026-09-04).

chromeTextStrong.$description: Copy button on hover/focus, and any titlebar affordance that must read as interactive. White at alpha/72 — 9.6:1 on code/shell.

chromeHover.$description: Titlebar affordance background on hover — the resting state is transparent, so this is the whole hover cue.

borderStrong.$description: Border of a titlebar affordance on hover/focus, where the resting code/border hairline is too faint to read as a control edge.

layer.$description: Nestable surfaces (Carbon's `layer` model). Each step is the background for content sitting ON the step below, so a card inside a card inside a page resolves by depth instead of by eye. `border/N` is the hairline that separates layer N from its parent.

on.$description: Guaranteed foreground for a given fill — Material 3's `on-` pairing. Every entry was CHOSEN BY MEASUREMENT, not by eye: the ink (dark or inverse) that clears AA on that fill in the WORST brand wins, because a pairing is only as accessible as its least accessible brand. This exists so a designer reaching for a status chip does not have to guess the label colour.

hover.$description: Ink on bg/neutral/hover — the body ink, because every neutral state fill is a light tint the same ink reads on.

active.$description: Ink on bg/neutral/active — the body ink, because every neutral state fill is a light tint the same ink reads on.

selected.$description: Ink on bg/neutral/selected — the body ink, because every neutral state fill is a light tint the same ink reads on.

readonly.$description: Ink on bg/neutral/readonly — the body ink, because every neutral state fill is a light tint the same ink reads on.

loading.$description: Ink on bg/neutral/loading — the body ink, because every neutral state fill is a light tint the same ink reads on.

blur.$description: Named blur strengths — UX4G 3.0's four semantic names over its own ramp.

icon.$description: Icon sizes: 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64. DBIM 3.0 section 3.4 (Figure 9) publishes four — 24, 32, 48, 64 — and all four are here. The other three are NOT a deviation to be corrected: 16px is the correct icon beside 14px body text and is the estate's most-used size, and DBIM 3.4 governs the downloadable asset bank rather than forbidding a smaller inline glyph. A standard's list is a floor, not a ceiling — see .claude/rules/standards-precedence.md. 24 is the estate default and the Material Symbols optical size <Icon> ships with. Each step is a FRAME: DBIM's four include 2px padding per edge, so their live area is size minus 4 (24>20, 32>28, 48>44, 64>60). Named for the pixel value on purpose — a t-shirt name can drift from what it renders, a number cannot.

16.$description: 16px — inline with body-2 and label text, and inside a chip.

20.$description: 20px icons. The Figma AccessibilityBar binds icon/size/20, so the step exists to mirror it. Note 20 is also precisely the LIVE AREA of a DBIM 24 frame (24 minus 2px padding each edge), so the rendered glyph matches DBIM's 24 step. Not a general-purpose step; 24 remains the estate default.

24.$description: 24px — the default: buttons, list rows, the masthead menu.

64.$description: 64px — the mark in an empty state or illustration tile.

size.$description: Icon box sizes, one per step the estate draws Material Symbols at. Each aliases `size/N`; 24 is the default `<Icon>` size and the only one most surfaces need.

fill.$description: Material Symbols’ FILL variation axis. 0 draws the outlined glyph the estate uses everywhere; 1 the filled glyph, for a selected navigation item or a toggled state where the same symbol must read as ‘on’. Code-only: the axis is set with font-variation-settings, which Figma cannot bind — the Figma Icon set carries Outline and Filled styles instead.

filled.$description: FILL 1 — the filled form of the same glyph, for a selected or active state.

container.$description: Page container max-widths. `sm`–`xl` carry UX4G 3.0's Bootstrap container ladder verbatim. `content` and `contentXl` are the estate's own page container — the pair a page skeleton actually binds. A container is a CAP, never a width: `grid/margin/*` is a floor that wins on narrower viewports, so the effective column is min(container, viewport - 2 x margin).

measure.$description: The MEASURE — the widest a run of body text may be. 36rem is about 68 characters of Noto Sans at 16px, inside the 45–75 the typography page requires and DBIM §7 asks for; in rem so a reader who raises their default font size keeps the same character count, not the same pixels. Added 2026-09-04: `.ds-prose` carried a 72ch literal, `max-w-prose` had four consumers, and the container ladder kept widening to 1376px while body stayed 16px — a 130-character line on a wide monitor. Bind prose containers to `--sa-container-measure`; Tailwind exposes it as `max-w-measure`.

sm.$description: 540px — UX4G 3.0's Bootstrap container step, carried for parity with the standard. The estate's own content column is `container/page`; use this rung only where a UX4G component is transcribed as published.

md.$description: 720px — UX4G 3.0's Bootstrap container step, carried for parity with the standard. The estate's own content column is `container/page`; use this rung only where a UX4G component is transcribed as published.

lg.$description: 960px — UX4G 3.0's Bootstrap container step, carried for parity with the standard. The estate's own content column is `container/page`; use this rung only where a UX4G component is transcribed as published.

xl.$description: 1140px — UX4G 3.0's Bootstrap container step, carried for parity with the standard. The estate's own content column is `container/page`; use this rung only where a UX4G component is transcribed as published.

2xl.$description: Completes UX4G's container ladder, which is Bootstrap's: 540 / 720 / 960 / 1140 / 1320. It was the one step missing here, so `contentXl` had to restate the literal; it now aliases this.

content.$description: The desktop content cap. Changed from 1280px to UX4G 3.0's published 1200px on 13 August 2026 ('Grid and layout': max content width 1200px desktop, 1320px desktop XL). Until then the estate ran FOUR widths at once — this token said 1280 and nothing consumed it, 22 website section files hardcoded the same 1280 as a literal, SiteHeader defaulted to 1320, and PortalLoginShell's chrome used 1536. The visible defect was that above 1320px the masthead's content ran 20px wider each side than the page beneath it, so the National Emblem did not line up with the content column. At the 1440 design frame 1200 leaves a 120px margin either side, comfortably clear of the 32px `grid/margin/desktop` floor. BIND `container/page` INSTEAD unless you specifically mean this rung: `page` carries a mode per viewport and resolves to the right rung on its own. This one is fixed at every window size.

contentXl.$description: The content cap above `breakpoint/desktopXl`. Aliases `container/2xl` rather than restating 1320, so the estate's cap and UX4G's ladder cannot drift apart. UX4G publishes the value but not the point at which it engages, so the anchor is the estate's own `breakpoint/desktopXl` — 1440 since 2026-08-24 (it read 1768, then 1600, before the page itself was measured). Bootstrap's `container-xxl` at 1400 was considered and rejected: at 1400 the 1440 design frame would take this cap, contradicting the 1200-at-desktop guidance. (This note said 1400 WAS the anchor until 2026-08-24; it never was — the token has read 1768, then 1600, and now 1440.) BIND `container/page` INSTEAD unless you specifically mean this rung: `page` carries a mode per viewport and resolves to the right rung on its own. This one is fixed at every window size.

contentWide.$description: The content cap at `breakpoint/desktopWide` (1920) and above — the third and last step of the page container (1200 -> 1320 -> 1440). Exists because two steps left a 2560-wide monitor rendering a 1320 column between 620px margins. Stops here rather than tracking the viewport: past ~1440 a 12-column grid costs more in eye travel than it returns in density, and the line lengths inside it stop being scannable. Consumed only through `--sa-container-page` in foundations/layout.css; never restate it in a component. BIND `container/page` INSTEAD unless you specifically mean this rung: `page` carries a mode per viewport and resolves to the right rung on its own. This one is fixed at every window size.

narrow.$description: AccessibilityBar narrow content container (Figma layout/container/narrow). Same 720px as container.md, named for the bar's own Layout variant.

wide.$description: AccessibilityBar wide content container (Figma layout/container/wide). 1200px is the Figma master's own value. It now COINCIDES with `container/content`, which moved 1280 > 1200 on 13 August 2026, but is deliberately left as a literal rather than aliased: the two are independent decisions that happen to agree today — this one is the bar's Figma master, that one is UX4G's published desktop cap — and aliasing would silently drag the bar along if the page cap moves again.

page.$description: The RESOLVED page cap at a given window size — what `.sa-container` actually applies, and the one container token a page skeleton should bind. `content`/`contentXl`/`contentWide` are the three rungs; this is which rung is in force. It carries a mode per viewport, so a designer opening a frame in Desktop XL sees 1320 without having to know the media query that picks it. That was previously impossible: the CSS derived `--sa-container-page` in a media query, and a Figma variable cannot express a media query, so the cap was the one layout value the library could not represent at all. $value is the mobile-first base, which is `content` — the cap is 1200 everywhere below 1600.

grid.$description: The LAYOUT grid. Geometry is UX4G 3.0's — 12 columns, a 24px gutter — because UX4G is the Government of India's own system and we hold a parity contract with it; a designer moving between the two libraries must not find a different grid. What is NOT UX4G's is the shape: UX4G expresses its grid as Bootstrap CSS classes, which is exactly why none of it ever reached Figma and why a designer had nothing to bind a layout grid to. These are tokens instead, per IBM Carbon's model, so the grid is bindable in Figma and auditable in code. Page MARGIN is deliberately responsive rather than Bootstrap's flat half-gutter (12px): 12px of breathing room either side of a government page on a 1280px desktop is too thin, and Carbon (32px) and GOV.UK (30px) both agree. Every value aliases an existing space step — no new literals. NOTE `grid/*` is the layout grid; `chart/grid` is a chart gridline COLOUR. Different objects, kept apart by position.

columns.$description: Column count, 12 — UX4G/Bootstrap. Divisible by 2, 3, 4 and 6, which is the whole reason 12 is the near-universal choice. Carbon's 16 (dropping to 8 and 4 at smaller breakpoints) is more expressive but would break UX4G parity for no gain the estate can use.

gutter.$description: The gap BETWEEN columns — 24px, UX4G/Bootstrap's 1.5rem exactly. Bootstrap applies half either side of each column; bind this as the layout grid's gutter and let the implementation split it.

margin.$description: The page's own side margin — the gap between the grid and the viewport edge. Responsive, because a margin that reads generous on a phone reads cramped on a desktop.

mobile.$description: BIND `grid/margin/page` INSTEAD unless you specifically mean this rung: `page` carries a mode per viewport and resolves to the right rung on its own. This one is fixed at every window size.

tablet.$description: BIND `grid/margin/page` INSTEAD unless you specifically mean this rung: `page` carries a mode per viewport and resolves to the right rung on its own. This one is fixed at every window size.

desktop.$description: BIND `grid/margin/page` INSTEAD unless you specifically mean this rung: `page` carries a mode per viewport and resolves to the right rung on its own. This one is fixed at every window size.

page.$description: The RESOLVED page margin at a given window size — the companion to `container/page`, and what `.sa-container` applies as its inline padding. `mobile`/`tablet`/`desktop` are the three rungs; this is which rung is in force. It steps with the CAP, not with the viewport anchors: a wider margin only buys breathing room while the container is still fluid, and once the cap binds it buys nothing and costs content. Stepping it at the desktop anchor did exactly that — content went 1152 -> 1136 crossing 1280 — so Laptop, Desktop and Desktop XL hold the tablet rung and the 32px step waits for Desktop Wide. Keeping 24 at Desktop XL is also what makes the content there exactly 1272 — the width the Handoff's own frame draws. $value is the mobile-first base.

layout.$description: Page-skeleton geometry — the measurements a shell needs that do NOT come from its content. `grid/*` describes the column system, `container/*` caps the content column, and this group holds the chrome around them. Only genuinely fixed values belong here. A masthead, a page header and a sidebar's own height all size to what they contain, so they are hugs in the component and carry at most a minimum here; a shell must never be laid out by subtracting a hardcoded chrome height. Measured from MoSJE-Portal--Handoff- node 2309:14405, a native 1440 x 1068 frame.

height.$description: The government accessibility bar. Genuinely fixed: it carries one row of controls at a known size, in every surface and every locale.

bar.$description: The accessibility bar's geometry — its fixed height, the one chrome measurement that does not hug.

chatbot.$description: The assistant's fixed geometry. The panel is deliberately NOT fluid: it is a viewport-level overlay on top of somebody else's page, so a width that responded to the page would move under the reader as they scrolled a different column. These five were authored in the Figma library first and had no counterpart here, which meant the master was bound to variables the stylesheet could not name.

width.$description: Panel width at rest. Wide enough for a 246px bubble to hold a readable measure and still leave the column its gutters; narrow enough not to cover the page it is helping with.

height.$description: Panel height at rest. A ceiling, not a floor: the panel caps against the shared corner rail via `100dvh - rail - launcher - gaps`, so on a short viewport it is shorter than this.

launcher.$description: Launcher diameter, and the closed widget's whole footprint. Well past the 24px WCAG 2.2 (2.5.8) target minimum, because it is the one control on the page a citizen may be hunting for.

bubbleMax.$description: Message bubble cap — 67% of the 368px content column, so the transcript never reads as a wall of text. CSS expresses it as the ratio rather than this number, so the cap follows the column if the panel width ever changes; this token is that ratio resolved at the default width, for Figma to bind.

typingDot.$description: Diameter of one dot in the typing indicator. Four of them, 110ms apart. Was recorded as 6 in the library while both the master and the stylesheet drew 5 — the variable was carried but never bound.

width.$description: The Indian flag mark in the accessibility bar. Fixed so the bar's left edge is identical across the estate.

flag.$description: The national flag mark in the accessibility bar — a fixed width so the 3:2 flag never distorts.

minHeight.$description: The brand row's MINIMUM, not its height. It hugs its content, which varies: two or three lines of ministry lockup, an optional BETA badge, a search field on the website, an account block on portals. 72 is the floor that keeps the emblem legible when the lockup is shortest. Never lay out against a fixed masthead height — see `layout/chrome/minHeight`.

masthead.$description: The masthead's minimum height — a floor for a row that otherwise hugs its emblem and title.

minHeight.$description: Accessibility bar plus brand row at their minimum — the offset the sidebar and content start at on a portal page. Use it for a scroll anchor or a sticky offset, NOT to size the shell: the brand row hugs, so the real value moves with the content. AppShell lays the shell out as a three-row grid (`auto auto 1fr`) so nothing subtracts this from the viewport. At the documented content the navbar measures 134 including its shadow, of which 118 is the layout box.

chrome.$description: The accessibility bar and brand row together at their minimum — the offset a sticky element or scroll anchor starts at.

width.$description: The portal sidebar's expanded width. Genuinely fixed: the nav labels are known copy, and a fluid sidebar would move the content edge on every route. Its inner padding is `padding/m` (16), leaving a 268 item column; items are `target/spacious` (48) tall. Below the tablet breakpoint the sidebar is not narrowed — it becomes a drawer.

sidebar.$description: The portal sidebar's widths, expanded and collapsed. Both are fixed so the content edge never moves between routes; below the tablet breakpoint the sidebar is a drawer and neither applies.

collapsedWidth.$description: The portal sidebar's collapsed width: a 56px icon row plus 16px padding each side. Fixed for the same reason as `layout/sidebar/width` — the content edge must not move between routes. Below the tablet breakpoint the rail is a drawer, never this width.

flyoutWidth.$description: Width of the panel a collapsed rail opens beside a Group item to list its level-2 pages. Fixed so the panel does not resize with its longest label.

login.$description: The authentication page split. Desktop is a 922 hero beside a 518 form panel; the panel insets by 64 each side leaving a 390 content column. These are genuinely fixed: the split is the design, not a consequence of content. Source: MoSJE Portal — Handoff, Login/Signup. Mobile drops the hero entirely, so none of these apply below 1024.

width.$description: Desktop hero column carrying the portal photograph, brand lockup and the signing-into bar.

gutter.$description: Horizontal inset of the form panel and the hero content. The space scale jumps 32 -> 120, so this sits between them deliberately.

width.$description: The form content column itself. 518 - 2x64 = 390. Every auth field, button and divider is this wide.

tab.$description: The two measurements a tablist needs that are not derivable from its content. Everything else about a tab — its height above all — is a hug of padding plus type, and must stay one: a fixed tab height stops the label growing when a citizen raises their browser font size.

indicator.$description: Thickness of the selected tab's underline or rail. Deliberately NOT `control/border/width`: this is a selection mark that happens to be a line, not a control edge, so it must not move when the form-control hairline is retuned.

track.$description: Inset between an enclosed track and the pills inside it — the track's own padding, and the indicator's top/bottom inset. Small enough that the track reads as a frame around the pills rather than a panel containing them.

target.$description: Minimum POINTER TARGET sizes. There is no single correct number, which is the entire reason this group exists as a ladder rather than one token: 44px is WCAG 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), which is Level AAA — NOT the AA floor it is usually quoted as. The AA floor is WCAG 2.2's 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) at 24x24 CSS px, and it carries a spacing exception: an undersized target passes if a 24px-diameter circle centred on it touches no other target's circle. GIGW 3.0 binds this estate to WCAG 2.1 Level AA + IS 17802 — and WCAG 2.1 AA contains NO target-size criterion at all, because 2.5.8 arrived in 2.2 and 2.5.5 is AAA. So every value here is a deliberate choice above the mandate, not a compliance minimum. UNITS: these alias the `size/*` scale, so CSS emits rem (1.5/2.75/3/0.5rem) and Figma receives the px equivalent (24/44/48/8). rem is the right choice and not an accident — a citizen who raises their browser font size gets proportionally larger targets, which a hardcoded px floor would deny them; at the 16px browser default the values are exactly the published numbers. Apple's 44 is points and Material's 48 is dp — equal to CSS px at 1x, but not the same unit, so do not treat the three as interchangeable when reading their specs.

min.$description: The absolute floor — WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA. Use ONLY where the spacing exception is genuinely satisfied or the target is inline in a sentence. Anything a citizen must hit on a phone deserves `comfortable`.

comfortable.$description: WCAG 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA, and Apple's Human Interface Guidelines minimum (44pt). The right default for a public government service: it clears the AA floor with room to spare and matches what iOS users' fingers are calibrated to.

spacious.$description: Material Design 3 / Android's minimum touch target (48dp). Use for primary actions and anything used one-handed on the move — this is the largest of the three published floors, so meeting it satisfies all of them.

spacing.$description: Minimum gap BETWEEN adjacent targets — Material 3's 8dp separation. It is also what makes WCAG 2.5.8's spacing exception reachable: separation, not size, is what stops a 24px target being mis-tapped.

elevation.$description: Which elevation a surface gets, by what the surface IS. The raw shadow ramp says how deep; this says what for.

inset.$description: Use for a surface that sits BELOW the page — a pressed well, a slider track, a recessed input. The only inset step; every other elevation lifts. Figma models it as the INNER_SHADOW effect style elevation/inset.

motion.$description: Motion by INTENT. You never pick a duration: you name what is happening, and the pair brings its duration and its easing together — a duration without its easing is half a decision. Twelve intents cover the estate (the previous five left components pairing an exit duration with an enter easing seven times because there was no hover intent). Every intent except instant and loading collapses to 0.01ms under prefers-reduced-motion; the build emits that block, so a component that binds a pair honours the preference without writing its own media query.

instant.$description: No animation at all: a checkbox tick, a radio dot, a state that must be true the moment it is set. Also what every other intent becomes under reduced motion. Bind it rather than omitting a transition so the choice is visible.

hover.$description: A colour, border or shadow responding to the pointer — the most common transition in the estate and the one it had no name for. Fast enough to feel attached to the cursor.

press.$description: Feedback for a press: the button's translate, an icon nudge, a card's lift. Emphasized so the settle reads as physical.

focus.$description: The focus ring appears instantly. WCAG 2.4.7 wants it visible the moment focus lands; a ring that fades in is a ring a keyboard user can miss. Bind this on outline and box-shadow in :focus-visible.

enter.$description: Something arriving — a menu, a toast, a panel's content. Arrives fast, settles gently.

exit.$description: Something leaving. Faster than entering, because the reader has finished with it and is already looking elsewhere.

expand.$description: A surface growing in place — an accordion opening, a drawer widening, a row revealing detail. The reader watches both ends, so it eases at both ends.

collapse.$description: The same surface shrinking. Slightly faster than expand, for the same reason exit is faster than enter.

emphasis.$description: A deliberate, attention-carrying move: a count rolling up, a chart mark drawing in. Reserve it — if everything is emphasised, nothing is.

reveal.$description: A surface the reader deliberately opened — a side sheet, a disclosure panel, the SAMAVESH banner. Arrives under its own momentum.

page.$description: A whole view changing: route transitions, a skeleton giving way to content, a step in a wizard. The longest move a citizen should ever wait on.

loading.$description: Indeterminate progress. These do NOT collapse under reduced motion — a spinner that stops is a page that looks frozen — so the build leaves them out of the reduced-motion block; components slow them instead (button.css uses 1.6s).

spin.$description: One revolution of a spinner. Linear, always.

pulse.$description: One breath of a skeleton shimmer, ease-in-out. Half a cycle each way.

stagger.$description: Cascading a list in. step is the delay between neighbours; max is the number of steps before the rest arrive together, so a long list does not keep the reader waiting. Under about 30ms the cascade does not read; over about 80ms the tail arrives after the reader has started looking for it (measured on the SAMAVESH banner, 2026-08).

control.$description: The shape of an interactive control. Density already moves a control's size; these are what it is shaped like, which was hardcoded per component.

radius.$description: Aliases shape/8, the system default control shape. Value unchanged at 8px. It previously aliased the Tier-1 radius primitive directly — a published variable pointing at one designers cannot see.

selection.$description: The selection controls — Checkbox and Radio. One family for the box, the circle, the glyph inside it, the edge around it, the corner and the gap to the label, so the two components cannot drift from each other. The row's HIT AREA is not here: it is target/min, target/comfortable and target/spacious, chosen per size, and the visually hidden native input is what fills it.

size.$description: The visible box or circle. sm 16 for dense tables and filter rails, md 20 as the default beside 14–16px body text, lg 24 where the box has to meet WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 on its own — the card variant and touch-first screens. Replaced a single hardcoded 18px that sat on no scale.

sm.$description: 16px box. Dense tables and filter rails, inside a 24px target/min hit area with target/spacing between neighbours.

md.$description: 20px box, the default. Sits beside 14 to 16px body text inside a 44px target/comfortable hit area.

lg.$description: 24px box. Touch-first screens and the card variant; the box alone meets WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8.

glyph.$description: The check mark or the indeterminate dash inside the box: the box less one border on each side. sm 12, md 16, lg 20 — the same steps as icon/size, so the glyph can be a library icon instance in Figma.

sm.$description: 12px check or dash inside the 16px box.

md.$description: 16px check or dash inside the 20px box. The same step as icon/size/16, so the glyph can be a library icon instance.

lg.$description: 20px check or dash inside the 24px box.

dot.$description: The filled dot inside a selected radio: half the circle, the ratio Material and Carbon both publish. sm 8, md 10, lg 12.

md.$description: A literal rather than an alias because no ref/size step is 10, and inventing one would add a scale step used by a single dot. Half of size/20, which is the md circle.

width.$description: 2px, up from a raw 1.5px. A 1.5px edge anti-aliases to a lighter, thinner line at 1x pixel density, and that rendered edge is the surface WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 measures a control's boundary against. 2px is what GOV.UK, USWDS, Polaris and Material draw, and it equals stroke/2 and focus/width. control/border/width stays 1px for text fields, whose edge is a frame rather than the control itself.

radius.$description: The checkbox corner. shape/4, not the 8px control/radius a text field uses: at 20px a box with an 8px corner reads as a circle, and a circle is the radio.

gap.$description: Between the control and its label. Was stack/8, a vertical token bound to a horizontal gap.

height.$description: Control heights — the three sizes a button, input, select or chip may be. md is the estate default and what density/control/height resolves to in Comfortable; sm is Compact's value and the dense-table control; lg is the touch-first size, which alone clears WCAG 2.5.5's 44px enhanced target. Bind these, not a number: a height typed once per component is how 32/40/48 drifted to 44 and 36.

sm.$description: 32px — compact controls, filter chips, table toolbars. Below WCAG 2.5.8's 24px floor only if the target has no spacing exception; give it target/spacing between neighbours.

md.$description: 40px — the default control height, and what density/control/height resolves to in Comfortable.

lg.$description: 48px — touch-first controls and primary actions on a phone; clears WCAG 2.5.5 (44px) and Material's 48dp on its own.

shape.$description: Tier-2 corner radius ("shape"). VALUE-NAMED: the rung IS the pixel value, matching the spacing ladder, except `full` — a sentinel meaning fully rounded, not a measurement. Apps bind these, never the Tier-1 ref/radius/* primitives. Named shape rather than radius because Style Dictionary merges the primitive and semantic namespaces, so a Tier-2 group called radius would self-reference the Tier-1 scale it aliases. ROLES live at Tier 3 (control/radius, cmp/*/radius) — that is why the rungs need not carry role names.

0.$description: No edge. Bind it rather than omitting a stroke, so an absent border is a decision and not an oversight.

1.$description: The hairline — the default rule weight. Dividers, table rules, card edges, documentation borders.

2.$description: A deliberate emphasis weight, for an edge that has to read at a glance.

3.$description: Heavy edge. Rare in product UI; check whether the emphasis belongs in colour instead.

4.$description: Heaviest edge in the system. Rare.

stroke.$description: Tier-2 border width ("stroke"). VALUE-NAMED: the rung IS the pixel value, matching the space and radius ladders. Named stroke rather than border because Style Dictionary merges the primitive and semantic namespaces, so a Tier-2 border/width/* would self-reference the Tier-1 border.width.* it aliases — the same reason the corner-radius group is called shape. It is also Figma's own word for the property (STROKE_FLOAT). Bind these for any rule, hairline or edge weight; control/border/width remains the right choice for an interactive control specifically.

0.$description: 0% — fully transparent — the resting state of a fade. Aliases `opacity/0`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

4.$description: 4% — the faintest wash — a hover tint on a neutral surface. Aliases `opacity/4`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

8.$description: 8% — the faintest wash — a hover tint on a neutral surface. Aliases `opacity/8`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

16.$description: 16% — a visible wash — pressed and selected tints, the overlay behind a popover. Aliases `opacity/16`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

24.$description: 24% — a visible wash — pressed and selected tints, the overlay behind a popover. Aliases `opacity/24`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

32.$description: 32% — a strong wash or a disabled element (`alpha/disabled` is 48). Aliases `opacity/32`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

40.$description: 40% — a strong wash or a disabled element (`alpha/disabled` is 48). Aliases `opacity/40`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

48.$description: 48% — a strong wash or a disabled element (`alpha/disabled` is 48). Aliases `opacity/48`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

64.$description: 64% — a de-emphasised but readable element (`alpha/muted` is 64). Aliases `opacity/64`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

72.$description: 72% — a de-emphasised but readable element (`alpha/muted` is 64). Aliases `opacity/72`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

80.$description: 80% — a scrim or near-opaque surface. Aliases `opacity/80`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

88.$description: 88% — a scrim or near-opaque surface. Aliases `opacity/88`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

100.$description: 100% — fully opaque — the resting state of an element that fades in. Aliases `opacity/100`; bind it to a colour alias's opacity for a wash, or to a layer's opacity for emphasis. Where the intent has a name (`alpha/disabled`, `alpha/muted`) use that instead.

alpha.$description: Tier-2 opacity. Each step aliases the Tier-1 `opacity/*` scale, the way `shape` wraps `radius` and `stroke` wraps `border/width`, so a designer binds `alpha/8` and never a `ref/*` primitive. Since 2026-09-04 every translucent colour token in the system (thirteen steps: 0 · 4 · 8 · 16 · 24 · 32 · 40 · 48 · 64 · 72 · 80 · 88 · 100) is a colour reference PLUS one of these — `color/transparent/accent/8` is `color/accentScale/600` at `alpha/8`, not a frozen rgba() — which is what lets a wash follow its base colour through a brand change, and what Figma's alias-with-opacity binding needs on the other side. In CSS the same token resolves as `color-mix(in srgb, var(base) calc(var(--sa-alpha-N) * 100%), transparent)`.

disabled.$description: A disabled control's whole-element opacity — 48% keeps the label's shape legible while making the state unmistakable. Prefer the opaque disabled ink (text/neutral/disabled) for text alone; use this only where a whole control dims (button.css, the accessibility bar's font-size buttons).

muted.$description: An enabled but de-emphasised element — an inactive tab's icon, a secondary illustration, a placeholder mark. Still readable: 64% of the body ink on white measures above 4.5:1.

z.$description: The layering ladder — the ONLY z-index values app code may write. Steps of 100 leave room for a local order inside a layer; anything a component stacks inside its own context (a caret over its own field) uses raised (1) and a literal 2 at most, never a ladder value. The four values above tooltip are the estate's fixed chrome and are named so nothing else can claim them: rail and launcher are the two floating rails (floating-element-placement.md), statutory is the UX4G accessibility panel's own 999999 — third-party, not ours to change — and demo/top are the DemoDock and the one panel allowed above it. Code-only: Figma has no z-axis property, so this group is deliberately not exported.

base.$description: In flow. Bind it to reset a stacking context something else raised.

raised.$description: One step above its siblings inside the same component — a floating label over its field, a selected tab over its rail. Local order, not a layer.

dropdown.$description: A menu, listbox or date grid opened from a control. Above page content, below anything sticky.

sticky.$description: A header, toolbar or table head that stays put while content scrolls under it.

fixed.$description: Chrome pinned to the viewport — the masthead, a bottom bar.

overlay.$description: The scrim behind a modal or side sheet. Pair with overlay/neutral/boldest.

modal.$description: A dialog or side sheet that owns the screen. Sits on its own scrim.

popover.$description: A popover, combobox list or date picker opened from INSIDE a modal — it must clear the dialog it was opened from.

toast.$description: Toasts and notifications. Above modals: a save confirmation must be readable even while a dialog is open.

tooltip.$description: Tooltips. Transient, pointer-anchored, above everything the reader can interact with.

rail.$description: The right-wall rail and its occupants (Important Links, DemoDock trigger). Fixed chrome that must beat product overlays.

launcher.$description: Closed launchers in the bottom-right corner rail — the chatbot button. Above the wall rail, and deliberately UNDER the statutory panel: a chat launcher has no business sitting on an accessibility control.

statutory.$description: The UX4G accessibility panel's own z-index. Third-party markup; recorded here so no SAMAVESH layer is ever placed at or above it by accident.

demo.$description: Demo scaffolding — the DemoDock. The reason this number is grotesque: it must beat the statutory panel while the estate is a prototype. Retire with the dock.

top.$description: The one layer above the dock: a panel the citizen deliberately summoned (the open chatbot). Nothing decorative may cover it.

aspect.$description: Aspect ratios for media wells — width divided by height, as CSS aspect-ratio takes it. Four, because a photograph, a video, a portrait and a square cover every media surface the estate draws; a fifth is a design decision, not a component's. Code-only in effect: Figma has no aspect-ratio property to bind, so these are exported without a scope.

photo.$description: 4:3 — the photo well in the geo-tagged photo and media-gallery inputs, the ratio a phone camera writes.

portrait.$description: 3:4 — a portrait photograph or an identity-document image.
